claims.text: Rapid quenching from the melt will improve both glass-forming ability and amorphous-state thermal stability in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
The starting material is a homogeneous phosphorus-containing alloy melt above its liquidus temperature.
The proposed intervention is immediate rapid quenching, such as water quenching, after melting.
The intervention should be effective when the melt is well homogenized.
The intervention should be effective when the cooling rate exceeds a composition-dependent critical threshold.
The intervention may fail when phosphorus content is far outside the glass-forming range.
Contaminants may promote heterogeneous nucleation and prevent the intervention from working.
Rapid cooling reduces diffusion and suppresses atomic mobility.
Reduced diffusion during rapid cooling limits nucleation of crystalline phases.
Phosphorus-rich clusters are particularly associated with the crystalline phases whose nucleation is suppressed.
Rapid quenching arrests thermally activated nucleation and freezes in a metastable amorphous structure.
Rapid quenching mitigates ordering by phosphorus and other alloying elements into crystalline phases.
The quench-generated structure will resist crystallization during subsequent thermal exposure.
Rapidly quenched samples will have a higher amorphous-phase fraction than slowly cooled samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will exhibit a higher crystallization-onset temperature or a longer time to crystallization during isothermal annealing than slowly cooled samples.
Conventional slow cooling is expected to produce a multiphase or partially crystallized microstructure.
Excessive phosphorus or impurities that significantly lower the required critical cooling rate could override the benefits of rapid quenching.
The exact critical cooling rate and magnitude of the thermal-stability improvement are unknown and require experimental determination.
Failure of rapid quenching to produce a statistically significant increase in both amorphous content and thermal stability relative to slow cooling would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that quenching works when the applied cooling rate exceeds the critical rate, but the boundary states that lowering the required critical cooling rate could override quenching benefits. Lowering the required critical rate would ordinarily make that condition easier, rather than harder, to satisfy.
